textRun.content: — a tour of the autonomous pipeline and the game I built with it.
SAY: "I ship at a rate that used to be impossible — and in twenty minutes I'm going to show you the harness that does it, not the hype."
DEFEND: Head of Vibe Coding at Snapchat, ex-Google. That's the only credential I'll assert without evidence; everything after this slide has receipts.
TRANSITION: "Five things, twenty minutes. Here's the map." -> agenda.
A game session that went somewhere I never coded.
One Slack message, the agent pyramid, and the loop that runs underneath.
How I work day to day
A real Slack thread and a real CMUX session.
The game, the rules underneath it, and the architecture.
Links, and how to play it.
SAY: "A story, how it ships, how I actually work day to day, the game itself, and where to find me."
DEFEND: Twenty minutes is the whole budget. This slide is navigation, not content — do not stop to explain any line.

WATCH: item 03 lands as the Slack thread (slide 7) and the CMUX session (slide 8) — those slides are tagged SLACK WORKFLOW and CMUX TERMINAL WORKFLOW, so say "this is the day-to-day part" out loud when you get there.
TRANSITION: "First — why you should believe any of this." -> credibility.
What I built with this stack —
Snap Growth Notifications, scaled to 5B+ notifications a day, ~100x growth from 2018 to 2026.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) connector to internal services
Engineers copy-paste between a browser tab and an AI chat window to pull internal data.
Stay in the terminal. The AI acts autonomously against internal services on your behalf and can drive tasks end2end.
Adopted by the majority of engineers
No path to remote-host an internal app — you either found a server or you didn't ship.
A shared server auto-registers and deploys your app — like a one-click internal app-hosting service.
Open-weight models as a frontier substitute
Internal benchmarks currently just matching SWE bench/online results, nothing interesting yet
Most open-model providers still lack full Claude Code / Codex API-level tool-use compatibility.
$70B+ paid to creators, 2M+ partners onboarded, $10B+ annual revenue at peak
SAY: "Before the toys: here's what the same harness-first approach did at scale, twice, at companies you've heard of."

DEFEND: Snap Growth Notifications scaled to 5B+ notifications a day, ~100x from 2018 to 2026 — Snap internal metrics, and the slide labels them as internal. Before that, YouTube Partner Program 2008-2018, founding architect. The $70B / 2M / $10B figures are public Google/YouTube disclosures, not my numbers.
HOSTILE Q "founding architect of what, exactly?" -> Name the one component you personally owned and shipped, in one sentence. Do not repeat the phrase "founding architect" as its own defense.
HOSTILE Q "adopted by the majority of engineers — out of how many?" -> "I don't publish Snap headcount. Call it widely adopted internally." Then move.
Pace: three cards, one line each. The BEFORE state is implied by the AFTER — do not read both.
TRANSITION: "That's the resume. Here's the thing that actually convinced me." -> the story.
Built AI world simulation -> The player tried to quit.
WorldAI is a live AI World simulator — the world reacts to plain language commands and remembers
Playing with my mom, her character tried to walk away from the business
The world argued back — saying if she tried to run away she’d go to jail since she has a lease and debt.
She stayed, and twenty scenes later she turned around her business.
REAL TRANSCRIPT · MICHELE FRIED CHICKEN CAMPAIGN
04 / 15 · the world remembers what you did
[~90s] COLD OPEN — the emotional beat of the talk. Slow down here.
SAY: "This is a real session I played with my mom. Her character owed a grocer named Mr. Park. She tried to walk away — and the world explained why that wouldn't work."

DEFEND: Nothing in that codebase has a "player tries to quit" branch. The lease, the loan, the police report — the model reasoned all of it from state it was already holding. Twenty scenes later she'd negotiated a 10% partnership instead of leaving.
Read one line of the transcript aloud — Marcus's line about the paper trail — then stop. Let them read the rest.
TRANSITION: "That's the product. Now the machine that builds it." -> pipeline.
all the way to green(magic, when it works)
A single natural-language message triggers the entire flow.
Bigger tasks still keep me in the loop.
Hermes pulls the relevant repo, docs, prior threads, and what your past goals were.
Orchestrator fans out to multiple worker agents in worktrees — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI — running in parallel.
Tests, lint, type-check, regression suite — all green before a human sees the diff.
PR lands with evidence bundle attached: logs, screenshots, git diff. No vibes, only receipts.
110 contributions a day · 19 PRs merged a day · 6 agent CLIs · 23 models
No manual re-entry of context, no babysitting CI, no chasing reviewers.
Full automation is the north star; on bigger tasks I'm still in the middle.
[~110s] THE VELOCITY SLIDE. Densest in the deck.
SAY: "One Slack message goes in. A green PR with an evidence bundle comes out. These five phases are everything in between."

DEFEND: 110 contributions a day, 19 PRs merged a day, 6 agent CLIs, 23 models. Basis: GitHub's own contributionsCollection API for 2026-07-25 to 08-25 — 3,402 contributions over 31 days. Merged PRs: 583 across non-fork repos, counted two independent ways that agreed exactly. Forks of other people's repos are excluded — cmux and hermes-agent are not in that number.
HOSTILE Q "are those actually YOUR commits?" -> "Agents wrote most of them. That is the point of the talk — I operate the fleet."
IF THEY QUOTE GITHUB AT YOU: GitHub's PR figure is PRs opened — 923, about 30 a day. My 19 a day is PRs merged. Both are true; they measure different things.
Say "Hermes" in phase 02 with a three-word gloss: "my Slack gateway — next slide."
TRANSITION: "The thing that receives that message is Hermes." -> what is Hermes.
that talks to everything you do
— and the agent stack that runs underneath them.
“Talk to your AI the way you talk to a teammate.”
Triggered the same way you message a person. No special CLI, no IDE plugin.
Hermes reads from everything you can read. Code is just one input.
“Replace more and more of your decisions over time.”
Each request reasons against your history, not a cold start.
SAY: "Hermes is one AI that reads everything I read — Slack, docs, calendar, error logs — and remembers what I decided last week."

DEFEND: Three properties, not three features. Frictionless I/O: you message it like a teammate, no CLI, no IDE plugin. Central data access: code is just one input. Memory: every request reasons against my history, never a cold start.
The diagram is a concept picture, not a map of the codebase — the footer says so, so you don't have to defend any box in it.
TRANSITION: "Here's Hermes doing real work, in a real thread." -> Slack workflow.
One thread → research → 99 replies of agent work.
Reply with the deliverable, no project tracking, no handoff.
SAY: "I saw a sprite-generation technique on X, pasted the link into Slack, and typed one line: let's test this out. Forty-five minutes later I had a comparison sheet."

DEFEND: 99 replies in that thread, and every one of them is agent work — research, iteration, generation. No ticket, no project tracking, no handoff. I replied to a message and got a deliverable back.
Point at the left panel, then the right panel. Two beats. Do not read the X post.
TRANSITION: "That's Hermes driving. Most of the time, though, I'm the one typing." -> CMUX.
in CMUX terminals most of the time.
drive them — and one pane sometimes runs multiple agents.
The default is me — I sit in CMUX and drive.
Well-scoped work goes to Hermes: it sends keystrokes into a pane, watches the output, and reports back.
One pane isn't always one agent — sometimes it's a manager spawning sub-agents inside itself.
[~90s] LIVE VIDEO — 45s of playback inside this budget.
CLICK IT. It does not autoplay and it needs live internet. If it doesn't load in three seconds, keep talking — the still frame makes the point on its own.
SAY: "This is my actual screen. CMUX is a terminal multiplexer where every pane is a git worktree with an agent living in it."

NARRATE — they cannot read that terminal text from row three, so tell them what they're watching: panes fanning out, each one a separate agent on a separate branch, and one pane that is a manager spawning sub-agents inside itself.
DEFEND: Manual by default, Hermes-driven on demand. One pane can be N agents. The isolation is per-pane git worktrees — that's why parallelism doesn't become merge chaos.
TRANSITION: "Underneath all of this is one four-tier structure." -> pyramid.
One cognitive task, tracked from dispatch down to tools.
A Slack bot handles dispatch — routing, task queuing, goal coordination — backed by an HTTP API gateway. Retains long-term memory and preferences.
Tier 02 — Orchestration (CMUX terminal manager & AO background daemon)
Two background services manage terminal panes, process groups, isolated code checkouts (git worktrees), watchdog restarts, and automated pipelines.
Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor CLI. Specialized workers executing code changes in isolated worktree sandboxes.

Short-lived tool specialists: Playwright browser testers, compiler drivers, BigQuery telemetry fetchers, test runners — some invoked via MCP (Model Context Protocol, a standard for AI-to-tool integration).
Isolated checkouts: orchestrator supervises, workers execute, subagents test.
What matters isn't # agents — it's the # cognitive tasks + context switches
SAY: "Four tiers, one cognitive task: Hermes dispatches, orchestration owns the terminals, CLI workers write the code, and short-lived tools test it."
SAY THE EXPANSION — the slide never defines it: AO is Agent Orchestrator, the background daemon that runs pipelines while CMUX runs the panes.
DEFEND: Every worker executes in an isolated git worktree. That single choice is why 10-20 agents in parallel doesn't collapse into conflicts.
Finish by reading the orange bar verbatim — it's the thesis of the whole talk: what matters isn't parallelization, it's the context switches forced on you.
TRANSITION: "So where does the human actually go?" -> left-shift / right-shift.
no human micro managing in the middle
Human focus allocation across the lifecycle. Front-load alignment, back-load verification.
Definition of done, verification criteria, evidence contract — before any code is generated.
Try your best not to interrupt the coding agent or watch every little thing it does, unless doing something brand new
Read the evidence report after AI evidence review, is your feature correct etc; failures kick back automatically. Code review comes last.
Cut human micro management to near-zero
— the human still owns the plan and the merge approval.
SAY: "I front-load the plan, back-load the proof, and refuse to sit in the middle refreshing CI."
DEFEND: Five minutes of planning on a small task, twenty to sixty on a deep one. That's the entire upfront cost, and it's what buys the hands-off middle.
Phase 03 is the one people miss: read the automated evidence report FIRST. If traces, screenshots, or benchmarks fail, it kicks back without me. I only read the code once the evidence passes.
Close on the Goal line: near-zero polling — the human owns the plan and the merge, not the grind between them.
TRANSITION: "Those three phases are six commands, and they're portable." -> skill system.
§ 11 · HOW I WORK DAY TO DAY
Six portable control points. WorldAI is the case study, not the prerequisite.
Fan out independent reviewers before you commit to an approach. /web-advice will use your browser window to avoid API cost
Recreate the exact failure on a real target, then fix its cause — not a symptom or a workaround.
Only a test you watch fail proves the bug is real.
unit → end-to-end → MCP/HTTP → browser. The first layer that reproduces the bug is the layer that owns it.
Every claim resolves to a real artifact. Looking verified is not being verified.
When it goes wrong twice, fix what let it happen — not the symptom.
Not shown: /web-advice, /dark-factory, /memory-search — real, but they depend on my own infrastructure (authenticated browsers, an external runner, a local memory store).
[~90s] PORTABLE SKILLS — the takeaway slide. This is what they can steal today.
SAY: "Six commands. None of them need my game, my company, or my infrastructure — they're prompts in a git repo."

DEFEND: /4layer is the one I'd argue hardest for. Unit -> end-to-end -> MCP/HTTP -> browser, and the first layer that reproduces the bug is the layer that owns it. That one rule kills most wasted debugging.
Second-best: /redgreen — only a test you personally watched fail proves the bug is real.
DO NOT point at the bottom-left "not shown" line; it collides with a URL there. The dark-factory link is on the closing slide anyway.
TRANSITION: "That's how I work. Here's what I built with it." -> WorldAI.
An AI Dungeon Master, playing live
Start a campaign in one sentence — the system generates the setting, your character, the rules, and the opening scene. The world reacts to what you do, and you don't always win.
You don't always win. Roll random dice + probably range
Factions act on their own goals. NPCs remember what you did weeks ago.
Rewrite your character, the world, or the rules in plain English. It persists.
Real session at worldarchitect.ai — server-resolved dice roll, XP award, and generated scene.
SAY: "One sentence starts a campaign, and the system generates the setting, your character, the rules, and the opening scene."
DEFEND: 14 specialized agents, 37+ prompt files. Bring your own key. It's live at worldarchitect.ai right now — say the domain without the http, the slide's scheme is cosmetic.
POINT AT the dice line in the screenshot: 1d20+1 = 18 versus DC 12. The server rolled that, not the model. That's the setup for the next slide.
Then God Mode — rewrite your character, the world, or the rules in plain English, and it persists.
TRANSITION: "Three pieces make that actually work." -> technical highlights.
Up to 300k tokens, bring your own key. A Min-first / Fill-to-max budget allocator: 40% story · 20% system · 5% memories · 3% npcs, remainder spills into story.
300k tokens · 4 components · bring your own key

Layer 1: FastEmbed, a small embedding model on my own machine, routes the request to an agent by meaning — local and free. Layer 2: Gemini 3 Flash, so only the right agent's prompt hits the paid model.
The backend provides a seed to the LLM and inspects the code after to ensure truly random. Probability range declared before the roll.
SAY: "Context budget, two-layer routing, and server-resolved dice. That's the whole trick."
DEFEND: FastEmbed runs locally and matches the request to an agent by meaning, so only the right agent's prompt ever hits the paid model. Routing is local and free; Gemini 3 Flash is layer two.

HOSTILE Q "<50ms local — measured how?" -> Name the measurement: local FastEmbed embedding inference on my own machine, not a network call. If you can't name it live, drop the number rather than defend it.

HOSTILE Q "zero fabrication? Really?" -> Do not defend the absolute. Say the real claim: "The server, not the model, resolves every roll. The model asks; code answers; the RNG provenance is in the audit trail."
TRANSITION: "Here's all of it on one page." -> architecture.
[~30s] POSTER, NOT A WALKTHROUGH. Do not trace any arrow. Hold, say one line, advance.
SAY: "Two engines, one gateway — and the server, not the model, resolves every dice roll."

DEFEND (only if asked): A faction battle or an intel action costs a SECOND Gemini call — the server runs the tool, then feeds the result back for narration. Pure-calculation tools are patched in server-side on Gemini 3 and stay at one call.

HOSTILE Q "12,378 lines in one file?" -> "That's the orchestration surface, it's under test, and splitting it is the next thing on my list. Judge the architecture, not the line count." Have that sentence ready — it's the likeliest attack in the deck.
TRANSITION: "Full-resolution version is linked in the footer. Last slide." -> links.
Let me know if you have any feedback on my game or harness!
Start a campaign in one sentence. Free for now — bring your own key.
One slash command drives a task from a spec to a green PR.
left and right shift your life!
, including the harness that built this deck.
Now go ship something at idea velocity.
SAY: "Play the game, take the skills, and tell me what breaks."
DEFEND: Free right now, bring your own key. dark-factory is the one-command idea-to-green-PR harness. jleechan-skills is everything else — including the harness that built this deck.
Pause on the QR for a beat so people can photograph it before you say the last line. This slide stays up through Q&A.
LAST LINE: "Thanks for watching. Now go ship something at idea velocity." Then stop talking and take questions.
[~0s] APPENDIX — skip in the live run.
Only reachable if you're asked a follow-up and want to jump. Say nothing here; advance straight through.
§ APPENDIX · THE EVOLUTION OF AI IN CODING
Four stages, less human at each.
→ less human, more autonomy, every step
[~0s live / ~45s if asked] BACKUP for "where is this all going?"
SAY: "Four stages, less human at each one. Most teams are at B — agentic shift, multi-agent, worktrees. The frontier is C: harness engineering, orchestrators managing 10-20 agents."
DEFEND: D — self-evolving systems that improve their own code — is labelled emerging on purpose. I'm not claiming it exists at scale; I'm claiming that's the direction.
Then return to your last main slide.
3 human-owned, 3 AI-owned steps, read clockwise back to step 1.
[~0s live / ~45s if asked] BACKUP for "how do you decide when to step in?"
SAY: "Six steps. Three are mine — quick plan, proof check, merge. Three are the AI's — async drive, evidence review, code review."
DEFEND: The human owns the entry and the exit, never the middle. That's the same left-shift / right-shift claim from slide 10, drawn as a cycle.
Then return to your last main slide; don't linger.
